anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > The mystery of the two earthquake pulses: "In 1900, British seismologist Richard Dixon Oldham analysed these worldwide seismogram traces."
purpose: Illustrate the historical hook: contrasting longitudinal P-waves (compressional ground oscillation parallel to energy ray) and transverse S-waves (shear ground oscillation perpendicular to energy ray) producing delayed arrivals on a seismogram record.
what_to_show: Diagram split into subterranean propagation and surface seismogram. Ray path travels upwards-rightwards from earthquake focus. For P-wave, double-headed arrow shows rock particle oscillation parallel to ray path; for S-wave, double-headed arrow shows oscillation perpendicular to ray path. Lower panel shows seismograph trace with baseline, sharp first arrival of low-amplitude P-wave, followed after time delta_t by larger-amplitude S-wave.
what_to_notice: Notice that P-waves arrive first because longitudinal compressional waves travel faster through rock than transverse shear waves. The seismogram trace shows distinct arrival times separated by time delay delta_t.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Transverse waves: "Top panel shows a wave travelling along a rope with perpendicular oscillations."
purpose: Teach the two-arrow classification routine by contrasting transverse wave motion on a rope with longitudinal wave motion on a helical spring.
what_to_show: Two comparative physical panels on white background. Top panel (rope): rightward green energy-transfer arrow labelled 'energy propagation', with a red vertical double-headed arrow at a marked rope point meeting at an explicit right-angle square marker labelled 'perpendicular -> transverse'. Bottom panel (spring): rightward green energy-transfer arrow with a red horizontal double-headed arrow collinear with the spring axis labelled 'parallel -> longitudinal'.
what_to_notice: The classification depends entirely on the angle between the two arrows: ninety degrees for transverse waves, and zero or one hundred eighty degrees (parallel) for longitudinal waves.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Compressions and rarefactions: "Along the stretched helical spring, coils crowd into compressions and spread apart in rarefactions."
purpose: Illustrate the physical structure of a longitudinal wave, showing alternating compressions and rarefactions in a spring and in an air column.
what_to_show: Helical spring with tightly bunched coils labelled 'compression (high density/pressure)' and widely separated coils labelled 'rarefaction (low density/pressure)'. Double-headed horizontal arrow across one compression to the next compression labelled 'wavelength lambda'. Double-headed arrow from compression to adjacent rarefaction labelled 'lambda / 2'. Individual coil marked with short back-and-forth oscillation arrow.
what_to_notice: Coils oscillate back and forth about fixed equilibrium positions while the patterns of compression and rarefaction advance along the spring. The distance between adjacent opposite regions is half a wavelength, lambda / 2.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Graphical representations of waves: "Checking the horizontal axis label determines whether the waveform reveals a wavelength or a period."
purpose: Contrast displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs directly, highlighting axis reading as the first diagnostic step.
what_to_show: Side-by-side graph comparison. Left graph: vertical axis labelled 'displacement y', horizontal axis labelled 'distance x'; dashed lines from peak to peak dimensioned as 'wavelength lambda'; caption reads 'Snapshot of many particles at fixed time t0'. Right graph: vertical axis labelled 'displacement y', horizontal axis labelled 'time t'; dashed lines from peak to peak dimensioned as 'period T'; caption reads 'History of one single particle at fixed position x0'. Both mark amplitude A from equilibrium to peak.
what_to_notice: Both graphs show identical sinusoidal waveforms, but their horizontal axes give completely different physical quantities. Distance gives wavelength lambda, while time gives period T.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Instantaneous particle motion on a travelling wave: "Figure 4.1 shows a transverse wave travelling from left to right with points R and T marked on the profile."
purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 2 evidence showing a transverse wave snapshot and the determination of particle motion direction.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/23/M/J/24 Question 4 Fig. 4.1 showing a sinusoidal transverse wave profile labelled 'wave' at one instant, travelling left to right as indicated by an arrow labelled 'direction of travel'. A horizontal dashed equilibrium line passes through the oscillation centre. Point R is located at a positive displacement crest; point T is located at an equilibrium zero-crossing on a rising slope.
what_to_notice: The wave travels horizontally to the right. Point T is at equilibrium on a rising slope, while point R is at a positive crest. Determining particle motion requires considering where the wave profile moves an instant later.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Instantaneous particle motion on a travelling wave: "Shifting the wave profile slightly in the direction of wave travel reveals the instantaneous motion of each point."
purpose: Demonstrate the wave profile shift technique for determining instantaneous particle velocity on a travelling wave profile.
what_to_show: Overlay of two identical transverse wave profiles. Solid blue line represents profile at time t0; dashed red line represents same profile shifted slightly rightwards by distance delta_x = v * delta_t. At point on rising slope, vertical downward arrow shows displacement decreases; at point on falling slope, vertical upward arrow shows displacement increases; at crest and trough, vertical displacement is momentarily unchanged (zero velocity).
what_to_notice: For a wave travelling rightward, the particle at point T on an upward slope must move vertically downward to reach the shifted dashed profile. Crests and troughs are turning points where instantaneous velocity is zero.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Longitudinal wave graphs and particle crowding: "Figure 4.1 displays a row of discrete medium particles aligned directly with a sinusoidal displacement graph."
purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 2 evidence showing discrete particles in a longitudinal wave aligned directly with a sinusoidal displacement-distance graph.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/23/O/N/22 Question 4 Fig. 4.1 showing a horizontal row of 14 discrete particle dots in a medium at time t0 aligned via vertical dashed extension lines with a lower sinusoidal displacement-distance graph. Direction of wave travel arrow points right. A downward-sloping zero-crossing on the graph aligns exactly with closely bunched particles at X (compression). An upward-sloping zero-crossing aligns with widely spaced particles at Y (rarefaction). Particle Z is located between a compression and a rarefaction.
what_to_notice: Bunched particles at X correspond to a downward-sloping zero-crossing on the displacement graph, not a peak. Widely separated particles at Y correspond to an upward-sloping zero-crossing.

anchor: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs > Longitudinal wave graphs and particle crowding: "Translating displacement values into actual particle positions proves that compressions form at downward zero-crossings."
purpose: Demystify the peak-equals-compression misconception by explicitly translating longitudinal displacement values into physical particle positions.
what_to_show: Three vertically aligned horizontal tiers. Top tier: 13 equally spaced dots representing undisturbed equilibrium particles. Middle tier: sinusoidal displacement-distance graph with positive displacement defined as rightwards (+x) and negative as leftwards (-x). Bottom tier: displaced particle dots showing actual positions. Vertical callouts prove that at downward zero-crossing, left particle moves right and right particle moves left, converging into a compression; at upward zero-crossing, left particle moves left and right particle moves right, diverging into a rarefaction; at crest and trough, neighbouring particles shift equally, maintaining normal spacing.
what_to_notice: A displacement peak means particles are displaced farthest to the right, but because neighbours move equally, density remains normal. Compression occurs only where particle displacements converge at a negative slope.
